title: Event logs, checkpoints and replay contracts
objectives: Define bounded versioned source/sequence event identity and exact duplicate/conflict handling without confusing command intent with external execution facts.

Use an explicit SQL transaction to commit event plus applied-cursor/projection together, demonstrate controlled rollback, and explain the additional file/settings/storage/recovery evidence required for durability.
Apply event logs, checkpoints and replay contracts invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: A log must explain what happened under which schema, source/session/order namespace and ordering rule. Include event version, identity, units, payload meanings and required historical rule/reference inputs.

blocks.md: A log must explain what happened under which schema, source/session/order namespace and ordering rule. Include event version, identity, units, payload meanings and required historical rule/reference inputs. A command is intent, not proof a venue accepted or filled it. Never reinterpret old payloads under new rules silently; define versioned readers/upcasters/migrations with retained originals and replay fixtures. Our count event (version, sequence, source, delta) is an own miniature schema, not FIX or a durable exchange journal.

Own schema 1, source SIM1, sequence 1..16, exact integer delta -10..10. Initial count 10; projection (value, through_seq) uses inclusive last-applied cursor. An exact stored sequence/content retry returns duplicate; different content conflicts; new events must be next contiguous sequence and keep count 0..100. One private database, one caller, one namespace, <=16 events. SQL primary key enforces sequence uniqueness here; real multi-source IDs must include the actual namespace. Malformed fields are rejected before beginning. Bound SQL parameters transport values; do not build SQL by interpolating event text.

blocks.title: Insert and projection are one commit boundary
items: Initial journal empty, through 0, value 10. Event 1 delta +2 commits both event row and projection (1,12). These must not be published as independent successful writes.
Event 2 delta +3 is inserted and projection changed to (2,15) inside an explicit transaction. Inject failure before COMMIT: ROLLBACK restores both to event 1/(1,12). No acknowledged append 2 exists.

Retry event 2 without failure commits (2,15); exact retry is duplicate, no extra delta. The demo remains in memory and disappears on close. Catching an exception is not an OS crash or power-loss test.

blocks.caption: Expected: appended; rolled back; 1 (1, 12); appended; duplicate; (2, 15). Python 3.12+ sqlite3, local tested SQLite 3.53.1. MEMORY database: SQL rollback/atomic event+projection demonstration, NOT file persistence, power-loss test or durable checkpoint. App runnable disabled until sqlite3/Python capability is verified. Single private connection/database; not an arbitrary schema validator or network broker adapter.

blocks.md: This example explicitly uses Python 3.12 sqlite3.connect(autocommit=True), then SQL BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT/ROLLBACK. In this mode Python Connection.commit()/rollback() have no effect, so do not replace the SQL commands blindly. No executescript is used inside the transaction. BEGIN IMMEDIATE can fail busy if a different writer holds the database; production retry must preserve identity, reload/revalidate and have bounded backoff. The private in-memory connection tests no competing writers. The transaction prevents the demonstrated partial local state, not unrelated external sends.

A recovery checkpoint must pair state with exactly the applied prefix plus schema/source/session/reducer/configuration. The projection row here updates its cursor and count in the same event transaction. Rebuilding from ordered events can independently verify that projection matches its prefix. A database WAL checkpoint is a different storage operation transferring WAL content toward the main database; it is not automatically an application snapshot contract. Do not conflate WAL checkpoint completion with authenticated coherent strategy state.

To persist beyond process exit, use a file-backed database with an intentional supported journal/synchronous policy, transaction completion/error handling, backups and tested restore. SQLite documents atomic commit and the assumptions it needs from OS/filesystem/storage flush behavior; turning off journaling/synchronization changes safety. A Python flush, successful close or renamed JSON file alone is not proof of durable event+cursor commit across power loss. Do not copy only an active database main file while omitting required journal/WAL state;use a supported consistent backup procedure. This lesson does not execute or certify file/WAL/backup/power-loss recovery.

A local COMMIT cannot atomically guarantee that a remote venue executed an order exactly once. If committed intent must later cause an external effect, use a separately specified durable outbox/effect dispatcher with remote-supported identities, retry/unknown-outcome policy and reconciliation. Replaying old events must rebuild local state without resending old orders. Checksums can detect some corruption but do not authenticate source or prove schema meaning. Reject/hold unsupported versions, gaps or conflicts rather than quietly skipping them while advancing the applied cursor.

Independent transfer: enumerate bounded valid delta logs, compare ordered event sum with projection, and repeat every accepted ID exactly. Inject failure after insert and after projection for every next event; check journal+projection unchanged, then retry once and compare with clean reference. Separately design file-backed process-kill/reopen tests and storage fault tests without calling controlled exceptions power failure. State exact durability settings and source boundaries before claiming recovery readiness.

Sources: [Python 3.12 sqlite3 transaction modes](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/sqlite3.html), [SQLite transactions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html), [atomic commit and storage assumptions](https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html), [isolation](https://www.sqlite.org/isolation.html), [PRAGMA settings](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html), [event sourcing tradeoffs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/event-sourcing). Concrete schema/bounds are own model. SQL transaction semantics do not turn this memory demonstration into a durable live trading service.

guidedExercise.prompt: Why is a successful in-memory SQL rollback test insufficient to sign off a durable trading journal?
guidedExercise.solution: It does not test file persistence, process/OS crash, power loss, journal/synchronous settings, storage flush behavior, backup/restore or concurrent writers. Need source/version/cursor consistency, reopen/crash/fault tests and reconciled remote effects separately. Controlled exception rollback proves only its tested local transaction boundary.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Event logs, checkpoints and replay contracts" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: Sequence identity is source-bound by this one-namespace private model; conflicts are not no-ops. (Identity and normalized content must agree.)
Do not elevate a local exception test into durability evidence. (Both local writes share one SQL transaction.)
realWorldApplication: Used directly across production quantitative research, execution systems, and validation pipelines.
quantFinanceApplication: Applies rigorous engineering contracts to quantitative modeling and live trading infrastructure.
summary: Versioned source-bound event semantics and consistent state/cursor matter.
Commit event plus projection in one local transaction; test rollback, duplicates and replay.
In-memory SQL, controlled exceptions and local commit do not prove file durability, power-loss recovery or remote exactly-once effects.

quiz.prompt: A stored sequence is retried with different delta content. What should this own journal do?
options: Treat it as an exact duplicate
Raise a conflict without committing a change
Append both under the same primary key silently
Advance the cursor and omit both
quiz.explanation: Sequence identity is source-bound by this one-namespace private model; conflicts are not no-ops. (Identity and normalized content must agree.)

quiz.prompt: What does this in-memory transaction fixture establish?
quiz.explanation: Do not elevate a local exception test into durability evidence. (Both local writes share one SQL transaction.)

quiz.prompt: After committed event 1 +2 from 10, event 2 +3 fails before COMMIT and rolls back. What value remains?
With autocommit=True here, which operation commits the explicitly opened SQL transaction?
options: Calling Python Connection.commit() instead of the SQL COMMIT command in this mode
Only updating the cursor in a different database
quiz.explanation: Transaction API semantics depend on the chosen mode. (Python Connection.commit() has no effect in this mode.)

quiz.prompt: Which input must a versioned replay preserve?
options: Only the event bytes, while silently applying the newest schema to old payloads
An arbitrary fresh random seed on each replay
quiz.explanation: Schema/source/configuration are part of replay meaning. (The reducer needs its actual determining inputs.)
